> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Its Lie algebra is $\mathfrak g=T_eG$, with bracket induced by left-invariant smooth vector fields. Fix also a finite-dimensional complex vector space $W$, a positive-definite Hermitian form $h$ on $W$, and a specified smooth group homomorphism $\rho:G\to U(W,h)$, where $U(W,h)$ is the group of invertible complex-linear maps preserving $h$. Thus multiplication and inversion on $G$ are smooth, $G$ is compact in its manifold topology, and every $\rho(g)$ preserves $h$. Every finite power $G^S$ below has the product smooth-manifold structure, with charts given by products of charts of $G$; for $S=\varnothing$, set $G^S=\{()\}$ with its one-point smooth structure. A **finite oriented lattice two-complex** is a finite set $\mathcal V$ of vertices, a finite set $\mathcal E^+$ containing one chosen orientation of each edge, an endpoint map $s,t:\mathcal E^+\to\mathcal V$, and a finite set $\mathcal F$ of faces. Each face $p\in\mathcal F$ is supplied with a based closed edge word $(e_1,\ldots,e_k)$ in the oriented edges $\mathcal E^+\sqcup\overline{\mathcal E^+}$, where the endpoint of each edge is the starting point of the next and the last endpoint is the first starting point. For the reverse orientation $\bar e$ of $e\in\mathcal E^+$, set $s(\bar e)=t(e)$ and $t(\bar e)=s(e)$.

A **link configuration** is a tuple $U=(U_e)_{e\in\mathcal E^+}\in G^{\mathcal E^+}$, with $U_{\bar e}:=U_e^{-1}$. The **holonomy of a face** $p=(e_1,\ldots,e_k)$ is the ordered product $U_p:=U_{e_1}\cdots U_{e_k}$ in traversal order, with the first traversed edge on the left. The vertex gauge group is $G^{\mathcal V}$ with coordinatewise multiplication; write $\mathbf e=(e)_{v\in\mathcal V}$ for its identity tuple. It acts by

$$
(h\cdot U)_e=h_{s(e)}U_eh_{t(e)}^{-1},\qquad h=(h_v)_{v\in\mathcal V}\in G^{\mathcal V}.
$$

Choose a normalized bi-invariant finite Radon Borel probability measure $\mu_G$ on $G$; explicitly, $\mu_G(G)=1$ and $\mu_G(gA)=\mu_G(Ag)=\mu_G(A)$ for every $g\in G$ and Borel $A\subseteq G$. The link measure is the finite product $\mu_G^{\mathcal E^+}$; for $\mathcal E^+=\varnothing$, this is the unit point mass on $G^{\varnothing}=\{()\}$. Empty sums are zero. Define the dimensionless lattice action and its normalized expectation by

$$
S_\Lambda(U):=\sum_{p\in\mathcal F}\Phi_p(U_p),\qquad Z_\Lambda:=\int_{G^{\mathcal E^+}}e^{-S_\Lambda(U)}\,d\mu_G^{\mathcal E^+}(U),\qquad \langle O\rangle_\Lambda:=Z_\Lambda^{-1}\int_{G^{\mathcal E^+}}O(U)e^{-S_\Lambda(U)}\,d\mu_G^{\mathcal E^+}(U)
$$

for bounded measurable $O:G^{\mathcal E^+}\to\mathbb C$. The finite-volume **Gauss sector** is the closed subspace of $L^2(G^{\mathcal E^+},\mathbb P_\Lambda)$ consisting of measurable functions with finite integral of $|f|^2$, modulo equality $\mathbb P_\Lambda$-almost everywhere, whose equivalence classes are invariant under each element of $G^{\mathcal V}$. Here $\mathbb P_\Lambda$ is the normalized probability with density $Z_\Lambda^{-1}e^{-S_\Lambda}$ relative to product link measure. For $v\in\mathcal V$ and $X\in\mathfrak g$, let $X^{(v)}$ be the tangent vector at the identity of $G^{\mathcal V}$ with component $X$ at $v$ and zero at other vertices. $$

a topological space $M$ satisfying:

derivations.claim: Fix a column $a$. The set $T$ of all horizontal edges together with the vertical edges in column $a$ is a spanning tree: each row is a horizontal path and the selected vertical edges join these row paths in one vertical path, with no other vertical edge in $T$ to close a cycle. Thus $T$ connects every vertex and has no cycle. The only inherited set-theoretic premise is $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ [A1].

In the finite-dimensional gauge-data instance, multiplication is continuous into $G$, so the inverse image of each Borel subset is Borel in the product topology. By [F3], this product Borel sigma-algebra is $\mathcal B(G)\otimes\mathcal B(G)$, proving the stated joint-measurability condition for that instance. The general compact-group argument below instead uses that condition as supplied data; it does not infer second countability for arbitrary compact groups.

Fix the root $(a,0)$ and set its gauge factor to the identity. Recursively along $T$, each tree-edge condition $h_{s(e)}U_eh_{t(e)}^{-1}=1$ determines the as-yet-unknown gauge factor at the next vertex uniquely, using multiplication and inversion in $G$. Hence every link configuration has a unique root-fixed gauge transform whose tree links are the identity.

First, inversion preserves $\mu$. For a bounded Borel measurable $f$, the map $(x,y)\mapsto(x^{-1},y)$ is measurable into the product sigma-algebra by [A2]. Composing it with the supplied measurable multiplication and then with $f$ shows that $(x,y)\mapsto f(x^{-1}y)$ is product-measurable. More generally, every finite group word in the coordinates is measurable, by induction using multiplication, inversion and measurable-rectangle generators. Since $\mu\times\mu$ is a probability, its absolute integral is finite by [F5]. Set $I:=\int_G\int_G f(x^{-1}y)\,d\mu(y)\,d\mu(x)$. Fubini [F6] permits either order of integration. Integrating in $y$ first and using left invariance gives $I=\int_G f\,d\mu$. Reversing the order and, for fixed $y$, substituting $x=yx'$ (again left invariance) gives $I=\int_G f((x')^{-1})\,d\mu(x')$. Thus $\int f(x^{-1})d\mu(x)=\int f(x)d\mu(x)$, so inversion preserves $\mu$. With root factor $h_{(a,0)}=1$, the inverse coordinate map is $U_e=h_{s(e)}^{-1}h_{t(e)}$ on $T$ and $U_e=h_{s(e)}^{-1}V_eh_{t(e)}$ off $T$. Recovering each $h_v$ recursively along $T$ uses left or right translations and inversion; recovering each off-tree $U_e$ from fixed $h$ and $V_e$ uses left and right translations. The forward and inverse coordinate maps are finite tuples of these measurable group words, hence form a bimeasurable bijection. The translations and inversion preserve each Haar factor, so successive finite Fubini integrations send $\prod_e d\mu(U_e)$ to $\prod_{v\ne(a,0)}d\mu(h_v)\prod_{e\notin T}d\mu(V_e)$; every bounded integrand used here is $L^1$ because all factors are probabilities. The tree coordinates integrate to $1$.

For each face based at $v_0$, substituting the vertex action from [F1] into its ordered boundary product cancels every intermediate factor $h_{v_i}^{-1}h_{v_i}$ and gives $U_p(h\cdot U)=h_{v_0}U_p(U)h_{v_0}^{-1}$. Since each $w_{i,j}$ is conjugation-invariant by [F2], the full density $\prod_{i,j}w_{i,j}(U_{p_{i,j}})$ is unchanged by the gauge-fixing transformation.

In tree gauge all horizontal variables are $1$ and $V_{a,j}=1$. The counterclockwise face word gives $P_{i,j}=V_{i+1,j}V_{i,j}^{-1}$. For a fixed row $j$, starting at $V_{a,j}=1$, the equations determine $V_{i+1,j}=P_{i,j}V_{i,j}$ to the right of $a$ and $V_{i,j}=P_{i,j}^{-1}V_{i+1,j}$ to its left. Thus the map from the $M$ non-tree vertical variables in row $j$ to its $M$ plaquette variables is a bijective triangular coordinate change. Both directions are finite group words, so [A2] and the finite-word argument of step 3.1 make it bimeasurable for the product sigma-algebras. Recursively, to the right of $a$ the map from $P_{i,j}$ to $V_{i+1,j}$ is right translation by fixed $V_{i,j}$, while to the left it is inversion followed by right translation by fixed $V_{i+1,j}$; both preserve $\mu$ by bi-invariance and step 3.1. Iterated Fubini therefore shows that this row map preserves the product probability measure. Distinct rows use disjoint vertical variables, so their product gives a measure-preserving bijection from all non-tree vertical variables to all plaquette variables.

By step 3.2 the gauge-fixed unnormalized density is $\prod_{i,j}w_{i,j}(P_{i,j})$. Each positive continuous $w_{i,j}$ is bounded above and below by positive constants: continuity gives a bounded neighborhood at each group element, and compactness gives a finite subcover; applying the same argument to $1/w_{i,j}$ gives a positive lower bound. Thus there are constants $0<m_{i,j}\leq w_{i,j}\leq M_{i,j}<\infty$, so the probability integral gives $0<m_{i,j}\leq z_{i,j}=\int_Gw_{i,j}\,d\mu\leq M_{i,j}<\infty$. In particular, each factor and the finite product density are $L^1$; Fubini [F6] applies to factor the partition function. The product Haar measure factors by step 4.1, so the partition function is $\prod_{i,j}z_{i,j}$; dividing by it yields the product of the displayed one-plaquette probability measures defined by the densities [F4].

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Use the matrix group $G_2=SU(2)=\{U\in M_2(\mathbb C):U^*U=I_2,\ \det U=1\}$ with matrix multiplication and the embedded smooth-manifold structure on $M_2(\mathbb C)\cong\mathbb R^8$ used for special unitary matrix groups. Its defining representation is the identity smooth homomorphism $\rho_2(U)=U$ on $W=\mathbb C^2$ with positive-definite Hermitian form $h(v,w)=v^*w$. In real coordinates every element has the form

$$
U(x)=\begin{pmatrix}x_0+ix_3&x_2+ix_1\\-x_2+ix_1&x_0-ix_3\end{pmatrix},\qquad x\in S^3:=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:\textstyle\sum_{j=0}^3x_j^2=1\}.
$$

Let $\sigma_3$ be the induced round surface-area measure on $S^3$, whose total area is $2\pi^2$, and let $\mu_2$ be the pushforward of $\sigma_3/(2\pi^2)$ under $x\mapsto U(x)$. In spherical coordinates $x_0=\cos\theta$, $(x_1,x_2,x_3)=\sin\theta\,n$, $0\leq\theta\leq\pi$, $n\in S^2$, its coordinate density is $d\mu_2=(2/\pi)\sin^2\theta\,d\theta\,d\omega_2(n)$, where $n=(\sin\varphi\cos\psi,\sin\varphi\sin\psi,\cos\varphi)$ and $d\omega_2=(1/(4\pi))\sin\varphi\,d\varphi\,d\psi$ for $0\leq\varphi\leq\pi$, $0\leq\psi<2\pi$. Define the real class function $\tau(U):=\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}_2(U)=x_0$.

For each oriented face $p$, let $U_p$ be the product of its link matrices in boundary traversal order, using inverse matrices on reverse edges. For dimensionless $\beta\geq0$, define the pure-gauge Wilson plaquette action on any finite oriented lattice by

$$
S_\beta(U):=\beta\sum_{p}\bigl(1-\tau(U_p)\bigr),\qquad \beta=\frac{4}{g_0^2}
$$

when a dimensionless bare coupling $g_0>0$ is used. The finite link measure is the product of $\mu_2$ over positively oriented edges, and its normalized expectation is the finite product integral with density proportional to $e^{-S_\beta}$. The one-plaquette normalizing factor and one-plaquette probability are

$$
z_\beta:=\int_{G_2}e^{\beta\tau(U)}\,d\mu_2(U),\qquad d\nu_\beta(U):=z_\beta^{-1}e^{\beta\tau(U)}d\mu_2(U).
$$

Since $\tau(U)=x_0\in[-1,1]$, every $\beta\geq0$ gives $e^{-\beta}\leq z_\beta\leq e^\beta$; hence $z_\beta$ is finite and positive and $\nu_\beta$ is a normalized probability measure.

This defines only a finite-lattice mathematical measure; it does not define an infinite-volume or continuum expectation.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and let $n\geq1$. Regarded as real Lie groups,

$$U(n)=\{A\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C):A^*A=I\},\qquad SU(n)=\{A\in U(n):\det A=1\}$$

have Lie algebras

$$\mathfrak u(n)=\{X:X^*+X=0\},\qquad \mathfrak{su}(n)=\{X\in\mathfrak u(n):\operatorname{tr}X=0\}.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix $n \ge 1$
and write
$$S^{n-1}:=\{\omega \in \mathbb R^n : |\omega|=1\}.$$
Let
$$\Phi:\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\longrightarrow(0,\infty)\times S^{n-1},\qquad \Phi(x)=(|x|,x/|x|).$$
This map is continuous. If $E\subseteq S^{n-1}$ is Borel, then
$(0,1]\times E$ is Borel and
$$\{r\omega:\omega\in E,\ 0<r\le1\}=\Phi^{-1}((0,1]\times E)$$
is Borel in $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ by
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]], hence Borel in
$\mathbb R^n$ by [[thm-borel-sigma-algebra-of-a-subspace-is-the-trace]]. It is
therefore Lebesgue measurable by [[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]].
Define
$$\sigma(E):=n\,\lambda_n(\{r\omega : \omega \in E,\ 0<r\le 1\}).$$

The next theorem proves that this is a Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ and that it
is exactly the surface measure needed for polar coordinates.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and $n\ge2$. The chart surface measure on $S^{n-1}$ equals the polar measure $\sigma$. Orthogonal transformations preserve it. The map $\omega\mapsto a+R\omega$, $R>0$, multiplies surface measure by $R^{n-1}$, and $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$.

A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where $[-\infty,\infty]$ has its order topology: finite open intervals and the endpoint neighborhoods $[-\infty,a)$ and $(a,\infty]$ form a basis. Its Borel sigma-algebra is generated by these open sets. A complex-valued function is measurable exactly when its finite real and imaginary parts are measurable, equivalently for the usual Borel structure of $\mathbb C$. Almost-everywhere assertions mean outside a measurable $\mu$-null set; completeness of $\mu$ is not assumed. Nonnegative extended addition uses $a+\infty=\infty+a=\infty$ for $a\in[0,\infty]$; positive scalars multiply $\infty$ to $\infty$, while $0\cdot\infty=0$. Signed expressions $\infty-\infty$ remain undefined and are not used in signed integrals. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
Closure properties of measurable functions used by the integral and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: In $M_2(\mathbb C)\cong\mathbb R^8$, the equations $U^*U=I_2$ and $\det U=1$ define a closed set, and $U^*U=I_2$ implies $\|U\|_F^2=\operatorname{Tr}(U^*U)=2$, so the set is bounded. By [F3] it is compact; [F2] gives the stated smooth Lie-group structure. It is noncommutative: $A=\operatorname{diag}(i,-i)$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ lie in $SU(2)$, while $AB=-BA$ and $AB\ne0$. The set-theoretic premise inherited by the lattice definitions is $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ [A1].

The coordinate map $\Xi:S^3\to SU(2)$, $x\mapsto U(x)$, is a bijection. Indeed, for $U=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\in SU(2)$, $U^{-1}=U^*=\begin{pmatrix}\bar a&\bar c\\\bar b&\bar d\end{pmatrix}$ while the adjugate formula gives $U^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}$, so $d=\bar a$ and $c=-\bar b$; unitarity gives $|a|^2+|b|^2=1$. Writing $a=x_0+ix_3$ and $b=x_2+ix_1$ recovers a unique $x\in S^3$, and direct multiplication shows every such $x$ gives an element of $SU(2)$. The map and its inverse are smooth coordinate maps. For round measure, use $x=q(\theta,\varphi,\psi)=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta\sin\varphi\cos\psi,\sin\theta\sin\varphi\sin\psi,\sin\theta\cos\varphi)$ on $0<\theta,\varphi<\pi$, $0<\psi<2\pi$. Its three coordinate tangent vectors are pairwise orthogonal with squared lengths $1$, $\sin^2\theta$, and $\sin^2\theta\sin^2\varphi$, so the induced surface-area density is $\sin^2\theta\sin\varphi\,d\theta\,d\varphi\,d\psi$. The chart boundary is a finite union of lower-dimensional smooth pieces and has zero three-dimensional surface area. Integration gives total area $(\int_0^\pi\sin^2\theta\,d\theta)(\int_0^\pi\sin\varphi\,d\varphi)(\int_0^{2\pi}d\psi)=2\pi^2$. Normalizing therefore gives $d\mu_2=(2/\pi)\sin^2\theta\,d\theta\,d\omega_2$ with $d\omega_2=(1/(4\pi))\sin\varphi\,d\varphi\,d\psi$, exactly the density stated in [F1], and total mass one. For $V\in SU(2)$, the maps $x\mapsto\Xi^{-1}(V\Xi(x))$ and $x\mapsto\Xi^{-1}(\Xi(x)V)$ are real-linear by [F6] and preserve $|x|$, since $\|\Xi(x)\|_F^2=2|x|^2$ and left and right multiplication by a unitary matrix preserve Frobenius norm. Their restrictions to $S^3$ are orthogonal transformations, which preserve round measure. Thus the pushforward formula [F1] makes $\mu_2$ a normalized bi-invariant Borel probability.

In the coordinates established in step 1.2, $\tau(U)=\cos\theta$. Because $\mu_2$ is a probability and $-\beta\leq\beta\tau(U)\leq\beta$, the continuous factor $e^{\beta\tau}$ is bounded between $e^{-\beta}$ and $e^\beta$; hence $e^{-\beta}\leq I_0(\beta)\leq e^\beta$ and $I_0(\beta)$ is finite and positive. The density $z_\beta^{-1}e^{\beta\tau}$ therefore defines the probability $\nu_\beta$ [F5]. The angular vector $n\in S^2$ has mean zero by the measure-preserving symmetry $n\mapsto-n$. The coordinate integrands are continuous and bounded on the finite product-coordinate probability domain, so they are $L^1$ by [F5]; Fubini separates the angular and radial integrals. The matrix coordinates then give $\int Ue^{\beta\tau(U)}d\mu_2(U)=I_1(\beta)I_2$, proving $\int U\,d\nu_\beta(U)=\lambda(\beta)I_2$.

The transformation $U\mapsto-U$ corresponds to the orthogonal map $x\mapsto-x$, so it preserves $\mu_2$ and sends $\tau$ to $-\tau$. Consequently $I_1(\beta)=\int\tau(U)\sinh(\beta\tau(U))d\mu_2(U)>0$ for $\beta>0$: the integrand is nonnegative everywhere and strictly positive on, for example, the coordinate region $0<\theta<\pi/3$, which has positive measure by the density in step 1.2. Also $I_0-I_1=\int(1-\tau(U))e^{\beta\tau(U)}d\mu_2(U)>0$, since $\tau\leq1$ and equality holds only at the identity matrix, whose singleton has zero round measure by the coordinate density. Thus $0<\lambda<1$.

The measure from step 1.2 is invariant under every orthogonal transformation of $\mathbb R^4$. Coordinate sign changes give $\int x_0d\mu_2=0$ and permutation symmetry makes all four squared-coordinate integrals equal; integrating $\sum_{j=0}^3x_j^2=1$ therefore gives $\int x_0^2d\mu_2=1/4$. Taylor's formula for $e^{\beta x_0}$ has a remainder uniform for $|x_0|\leq1$ on a neighborhood of $\beta=0$; its integrals are finite because $\mu_2$ is a probability. Odd moments vanish under $x_0\mapsto-x_0$. Thus $I_0(\beta)=1+\beta^2/8+O(\beta^4)$ and $I_1(\beta)=\beta/4+O(\beta^3)$, so division gives $\lambda(\beta)=\beta/4+O(\beta^3)$.

Assume the axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Fix the compact noncommutative finite-dimensional real Lie group $G$ supplied by the earlier non-Abelian gauge-data definition. A **finite oriented lattice two-complex** is a finite set $\mathcal V$ of vertices, a finite set $\mathcal E^+$ containing one chosen orientation of each edge, an endpoint map $s,t:\mathcal E^+\to\mathcal V$, and a finite set $\mathcal F$ of faces. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M,N\geq1$ be integers and use the finite $M$-by-$N$ square lattice with free boundary (no periodic identifications and all boundary links retained). Its vertices are $(i,j)$ for $0\leq i\leq M$, $0\leq j\leq N$; its positively oriented edges are eastward $h_{i,j}:(i,j)\to(i+1,j)$ for $0\leq i<M$, $0\leq j\leq N$, and northward $v_{i,j}:(i,j)\to(i,j+1)$ for $0\leq i\leq M$, $0\leq j<N$; and its faces $p_{i,j}$ for $0\leq i<M$, $0\leq j<N$ have counterclockwise boundary words $(h_{i,j},v_{i+1,j},\bar h_{i,j+1},\bar v_{i,j})$. Use the matrix group $SU(2)=\{U\in M_2(\mathbb C):U^*U=I_2,\det U=1\}$ with matrix multiplication and its identity defining representation. In real coordinates its elements are

$$
U(x)=\begin{pmatrix}x_0+ix_3&x_2+ix_1\\-x_2+ix_1&x_0-ix_3\end{pmatrix},\qquad x\in S^3:=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:\textstyle\sum_{j=0}^3x_j^2=1\}.
$$

Let $\sigma_3$ be the induced round surface-area measure on $S^3$, with total area $2\pi^2$, and let $\mu_2$ be the pushforward of $\sigma_3/(2\pi^2)$ under this map. Each positively oriented edge carries one link matrix; reverse links use inverses. For each face $p$, $U_p$ is the product of its boundary links in traversal order; for a loop $C$, $U_C$ is the analogous ordered edge product. Use the Wilson action $S_\beta(U)=\beta\sum_p(1-\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}_2 U_p)$ and normalized loop $W(C)=\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}_2 U_C$. Let $\beta=4/g_0^2$ for dimensionless $g_0>0$, and restrict to the explicit strong-coupling window $0<\beta\leq1$ (equivalently $g_0^2\geq4$). For any axis-aligned rectangle contained in the lattice with corners $(a,c)$ and $(b,d)$, where $0\leq a<b\leq M$ and $0\leq c<d\leq N$, let $C_{a,b;c,d}$ be its boundary traversed counterclockwise from $(a,c)$. Its area in plaquette units is $A=(b-a)(d-c)$. Define $Z(SU(2)):=\{z\in SU(2):zU=Uz\text{ for every }U\in SU(2)\}$ and $\chi:Z(SU(2))\to\{\pm1\}$ by $z=\chi(z)I_2$. $$

$$

$$

$$
